nature-eco-560.title: Fire as the boreal forest's renewal
nature-eco-560.text: Boreal fires often burn more than 10,000 ha, and sometimes more than 400,000 ha. Fire is the main disturbance that renews boreal forest stands, and an area's fire regime describes the type, size and frequency of its fires. The boreal regime is dominated by intense crown fires, which race through the treetops, or by severe fires along the ground. Fire rotation is the average time it takes for fires to burn an area equal to the whole ecosystem; individual sites may be skipped or burn more often. In lichen woodland, large damaging fires recur roughly every 70 to 100 years.

nature-eco-476.title: Mire, bog and fen: sorting the peatlands
nature-eco-476.text: Ecologists call any land with at least 30 cm of peat a peatland, even if it has been drained. A mire is a peatland still forming peat. It comes in two types. A bog sits higher than its surroundings and gets all its water from rain and snow. A fen lies on a slope, flat or hollow and gets most of its water from surrounding soil or water underground. In both, water passing through peat loses nutrients and becomes more acidic, so mires are usually nutrient-poor.

nature-eco-479.title: Palm oil on peat: profit against carbon and fire
nature-eco-479.text: Palm oil needs only 0.26 hectares of land to produce 1 ton of oil, and it has given income to smallholders in countries such as Indonesia and Malaysia. In Southeast Asia, that profit has a cost. Large areas of peatland forest have been drained and cleared for palm oil, trading economic gains against losses of carbon, biodiversity and safety from fire. About 12.9 Mha, about 47% of Southeast Asian peatlands, had been deforested by 2006. Emissions from palm oil on peatland are estimated at 12.4 to 76.6 t CO2/ha, and converted land can stay a carbon source after 12 years. Drained peat dries into a flammable layer, and its fires cause thousands of deaths each year.

nature-eco-480.title: Tropical peat fires: smoke across borders
nature-eco-480.text: Southeast Asian tropical peatlands cover only 0.2% of land but emit an estimated 2 Gt CO2 a year, equal to 7% of global fossil fuel emissions. Once drained and cleared, these peatlands burn increasingly often, releasing huge amounts of carbon dioxide. A severe fire can release up to 4,000 t of CO2/ha, and such fires usually burn for 1–3 months. More than 2 million hectares burned in Southeast Asia in the past ten years. The smoke does not stay home: peat fires send it across international borders almost every year.

nature-eco-426.title: Kelp as a carbon sink
nature-eco-426.text: Macroalgae, the large seaweeds such as kelp, take up 200 million tons of carbon dioxide every year. Kelp absorbs carbon as it grows. When it sinks to the deep ocean floor, that carbon can stay stored, far from human disturbance. Around Australia, kelp forests were estimated to store 1.3-2.8 teragrams of carbon per year, 27–34% of the carbon the continent's coastal habitats store each year, its {{ref:nature-nbs-034}}.

nature-eco-423.title: The layers of a kelp forest
nature-eco-423.text: Giant kelp grows tall enough to form floating canopies at the ocean surface. A kelp forest is built in layers, from these canopy kelps down to kelps and algae on the sea floor, and its structure decides which species live there. Below the canopy, stipitate kelps stand a few meters above the sea floor, and prostrate kelps lie along it; together they form the understory. Beneath them lies a bottom layer of other algae and attached animals.

nature-eco-510.title: Cutting peat for fuel and gardens
nature-eco-510.text: Peat supplies more than 20% of home heat in Ireland, and it is burned for fuel in Finland, Scotland, Germany and Russia. Peat extraction means cutting peat from bogs to burn as fuel or to sell as a garden soil improver. Russia is the leading exporter of fuel peat, at more than 90 million metric tons per year. Peat builds up so slowly that a bog is hard to restore once the peat is gone. More than 90% of England's bogs have been damaged or destroyed, and in 2011 the UK announced plans to remove peat from gardening products.

nature-eco-512.title: Bogs drying, draining and warming
nature-eco-512.text: Many Arctic and sub-Arctic bogs are warming at 0.6 °C per decade, twice the global average, and releasing large amounts of greenhouse gases. Bogs take thousands of years to form and are very hard to recover, yet drying, drainage and warming are degrading them. Northern European sphagnum bogs were often cleared and drained for farming. European peatlands have dried quickly in recent centuries from drainage, peat cutting and burning. These changes have caused severe declines in peatland biodiversity across Northern Europe. Many agencies now treat bogs as priority habitats, including the UK's national plan for wildlife ({{ref:nature-gov-043}}).

nature-eco-509.title: Raised, blanket, quaking: kinds of bog
nature-eco-509.text: A quaking bog is a floating mat of moss and sedge, about half a meter thick, that moves when someone walks on it. Bogs are classed by landscape position, water source and nutrient supply. Valley bogs form in gently sloping hollows; because they rely on ground or surface water, they occur only on acidic ground. Raised bogs grow over centuries from a lake, through marsh and fen, until a rain-fed peat dome a few meters high forms. Blanket bogs cover hilltops and slopes in cool places with rain on more than c. 235 days a year.

nature-eco-489.title: How seagrass shields the shore
nature-eco-489.text: Without seagrass, currents carry seafloor sediment away and erode the bottom. Seagrass leaves and roots calm waves and hold sediment, protecting coasts from erosion and storm-driven high water. Seagrass is an ecosystem engineer that reshapes their surroundings physically and chemically. Their leaves slow currents so sediment settles and builds up the seafloor. By reducing wave energy and building sediment, they protect houses and cities from the sea and from rising sea levels.

nature-eco-490.title: Seagrass: where fisheries begin
nature-eco-490.text: About half of global fisheries are estimated to get their start in seagrass habitats. Lose the seagrass, and the fisheries go too. Seagrass meadows are sheltered nurseries for young fish and shellfish that later support fishing. They give young fish a home in over 1/5th of the world's 25 largest fisheries, including walleye pollock, the most landed species. Gleaning shellfish by hand in seagrass exposed at low tide feeds hundreds of millions of people, and small-scale seagrass fishing acts as a safety net for the poor. Yet a 2019 study found this role is poorly reflected in the decisions of the authorities who manage seagrass.

nature-eco-493.title: Replanting lost seagrass
nature-eco-493.text: In Chesapeake Bay, several million eelgrass seeds are gathered each year with a mechanical harvester. Seagrass restoration re-establishes lost beds by transplanting plants or sowing seeds and other propagules, the plant parts that can grow into new plants. Communities in Virginia, Florida, Hawaii and the United Kingdom are restoring beds lost to human activity, and reintroductions improve ecosystem services. Most projects use cuttings, rhizome fragments or cores taken from donor meadows; few use seeds. Seed-based restoration has had low and variable results, with more than 90% of propagules failing to survive.

nature-eco-492.title: Wasting disease: a slime mold that kills eelgrass
nature-eco-492.text: After the 2015–2016 northeast Pacific heatwave, the share of eelgrass infected by wasting disease rose from 5–70% in 2013 to 60–90% by 2017. Over the same period eelgrass shoot density fell by 60%. Seagrass wasting disease attacks eelgrass, the most widespread seagrass, and is caused by the marine slime mold Labyrinthula zosterae. The pathogen enters leaf tissue, impairs photosynthesis and breaks down cells, leaving dark spots and streaks. Warmer seas fuel outbreaks. Meadows with little disease may mark refuges that can withstand climate change, worth putting first for protection and restoration.

nature-eco-544.title: The intertidal zone: between high and low tide
nature-eco-544.text: Some shore animals spend part of every day out of the water. The intertidal zone is the shore area exposed to air at low tide and covered by seawater at high tide. It is divided into the spray zone and the high, middle and low intertidal zones, each with its own conditions and wildlife. The high zone's changing conditions favour hardy animals such as barnacles, snails, mussels and hermit crabs. The low zone is almost always under water, and life is more abundant there.

nature-eco-542.title: Mangrove forests: carbon-rich nurseries of the tropics
nature-eco-542.text: The world's largest mangrove forest, the Sundarbans, covers 10,000 km2 in the Ganges–Brahmaputra delta. Mangrove forests are productive wetlands of salt-tolerant trees growing in tropical and subtropical intertidal zones. About 80 mangrove species exist. They cannot survive freezing, which keeps them in warm climates. Their stilt-like roots slow tidal water so sediment settles, forming a barrier that reduces erosion of the shore by waves and storm-driven high water. The roots shelter many species and act as nurseries for young fish, including commercially important ones. Mangroves are among the most productive ecosystems, with net primary productivity of about 208 Tg C per year, and they generally take up more carbon than they release. They sequester over 25 million tons of carbon each year, so losing them reduces carbon storage. Losses are heavy. Where data exist, about 35% of mangroves have been destroyed, and around 2% of mangrove area has been lost each year since the 1980s. Shrimp farming causes about a quarter of the destruction, and fish farming, oil and timber production have also driven losses.

nature-eco-549.title: Mudflats: the shorebirds' refuelling stations
nature-eco-549.text: Tens of millions of migratory shorebirds depend on mudflats as stopovers between their breeding and non-breeding areas. Mudflats, or tidal flats, are coastal wetlands formed in intertidal areas where tides or rivers have deposited sediment. A 2019 global analysis found they are as extensive as mangroves, covering at least 127,921 km2, with 44% in Asia. Once seen as economically unimportant, they were often dredged or converted to farmland. Up to 16% of the world's tidal flats have disappeared since the mid-1980s. Around the Yellow Sea, more than 65% of the mudflats present in the early 1950s had been destroyed by the late 2000s.

nature-eco-545.title: Vegetated coasts: seagrass, mangrove and marsh together
nature-eco-545.text: Seagrass beds, mangrove forests and tidal marshes together cover about 50 million hectares. These plant-dominated shore habitats are known as vegetated coastal ecosystems. They provide fish production, coastline protection, pollution buffering and high carbon storage. Their secret lies below. They sit on organic-rich sediments, sometimes metres deep, whose carbon stocks can be several times those of forests. When they are degraded or converted, that sediment is exposed to oxygen, and microbes release large amounts of greenhouse gases. They are being lost to fish farming, agriculture, dams, dredging, eutrophication, urban development and rising seas.

nature-eco-488.title: Seagrass blue carbon: burying carbon in the seabed
nature-eco-488.text: Seagrass meadows cover only 0.1% of the ocean floor yet account for 10–18% of all carbon buried in the ocean. Seagrass blue carbon is the carbon dioxide these meadows pull from the air and bury in seabed sediment, part of the coastal carbon store called {{ref:nature-nbs-034}}. Per hectare, seagrass holds twice as much carbon dioxide as rain forests, and meadows can take up about 27 million tons of CO2 a year. Global meadows are estimated to store up to 19.9 Pg (billion tons) of organic carbon. The trick is in the mud. Carbon builds up in low-oxygen seabed sediments, where slow decomposition preserves it for decades to millennia. Land habitats lose carbon to decay, fire or deforestation; marine sinks can keep it far longer. Burial rates vary with species, sediment and depth, averaging about 140 g C m−2 yr−1. Restoration works on a human timescale too. Restored seagrass meadows began storing carbon in sediment within about four years.

nature-eco-543.title: The outwelling hypothesis: mangroves feeding the coast
nature-eco-543.text: A mature mangrove forest reaches its maximum biomass after about 20–30 years. After that, the carbon it keeps fixing must be stored in sediment, exported or lost to the air. The outwelling hypothesis holds that much of it is exported as organic matter that feeds detritus-based food webs, which run on dead material, in nearby coastal habitats. Mass-balance studies, which add up carbon going in and out, support the idea. Mangroves usually fix far more carbon than they store, though the amount exported varies a lot between forests.

nature-eco-547.title: Reefs, seagrass and mangroves as one system
nature-eco-547.text: Protecting fish in a mangrove can raise fish numbers on a nearby reef. Coral reefs, seagrasses and mangroves are linked systems that shield one another and exchange fish and invertebrates. Mangroves and seagrasses regulate the sediment, freshwater and nutrients that reach coral reefs. Their ecosystem services reinforce each other: protecting fisheries in one raises fish biomass in the others, and tourism gains from both.

nature-eco-555.title: Five depth zones of the open ocean
nature-eco-555.text: The open ocean is divided by depth into five layers: epipelagic, mesopelagic, bathypelagic, abyssopelagic and hadopelagic. The sunlit epipelagic zone is the only layer with enough light for photosynthesis. Nearly all ocean primary production and about 90% of marine life are found there. The twilight mesopelagic zone gets only trace sunlight; many of its animals make their own light or rise to the surface at night to feed. In the pitch-black bathypelagic zone most animals live on 'marine snow', detritus falling from above. The hadal zone, below 6,000 m in trenches, reaches 10,935 m at Challenger Deep, with pressures of 1,100 atm.

nature-eco-566.title: Permafrost thaw: warming that feeds itself
nature-eco-566.text: The IPCC estimates permafrost emissions at 14–175 billion tonnes of CO2-equivalent per 1 °C of warming, against about 40 billion tonnes of human CO2 emissions in 2019. Permafrost is ground that stays frozen year-round. As warming thaws it, stored carbon escapes as greenhouse gases that cause more warming and more thaw, a positive feedback. A 2018 article suggested that at about 2 °C of warming, permafrost thaw would add a further 0.09 °C (range 0.04–0.16 °C) by 2100. Thaw also threatens roads, pipelines and other infrastructure built on frozen ground.

nature-eco-537.title: From bog to rich fen: a gradient of species
nature-eco-537.text: Calcium-rich water can turn a peatland from a species-poor bog into a species-rich fen. The bog–rich-fen gradient arranges peatlands from species-poor bogs, through poor fens, to species-rich fens. Where a site falls depends strongly on its pH and on calcium and bicarbonate levels. Rich fens get much of their water from mineral-rich sources, and their near-neutral water supports high biodiversity. Poor fens are more acidic, with a pH of about 5.5 to 4, and their thicker peat cuts plants off from the mineral soil below.

nature-eco-527.title: Is the Sahel really turning to desert
nature-eco-527.text: The Sahel, in Africa, has greened over recent decades. That fact sits awkwardly with a familiar story of spreading deserts, and the dispute over whether that story is accurate is the desertification narrative debate. Desertification is a real and major threat to ecosystems and people, worst in Western Asia and South America. Critics say the Sahel is wrongly seen as drying faster than elsewhere, a view they trace to colonial readings of how local people used the land. Researchers remain divided, and the dominant narrative for the Sahel is contested rather than settled.

nature-eco-523.title: What drylands give the world
nature-eco-523.text: Millions of people in developing countries rely on dryland ecosystems for a secure food supply and a good life. Drylands provide food, livelihoods, carbon storage and biodiversity, both to local people and to the world. Dryland ways of life help slow climate change by locking away carbon, and they conserve species. Drylands provide significant global economic value through their ecosystem services and biodiversity. The {{ref:nature-hist-008}} conference in June 2012 also stressed that dryland biodiversity is worth protecting for its own sake.

nature-eco-521.title: From sub-humid to hyper-arid: grading drylands
nature-eco-521.text: Arid lands cover about 10% of the world's land and hold 20% of its people. Drylands are graded into four classes by aridity: dry sub-humid, semi-arid, arid and hyper-arid. Dry sub-humid lands produce a large share of the world's crops and livestock. By one rainfall-based measure, semi-arid lands get between 500 and 800mm a year. Arid lands have an aridity index of ~0.05-0.20 under the UNCCD, the UN treaty on desertification. Hyper-arid lands cover ~8% of the world and get barely more than 100 mm of rain; the UNCCD leaves them out of its dryland definition.

nature-eco-522.title: Drylands in a warming world
nature-eco-522.text: From 1982 to 2015, 12.6% of the world's drylands degraded because of human-caused climate change. Climate change and human activity are degrading drylands, bringing more drought, desertification and erosion. About 7.6% of global land has recently turned drier, an area larger than Canada. Dryland degradation and desertification affect 213 million people, mostly in the Global South, and threaten people's food supply. People are adapting. Herders move their herds earlier, keep smaller herds, change how they manage water and vary their migration routes. Mobile herding and other sustainable land management, restoration and climate-smart farming can soften the impacts.

nature-eco-524.title: Restoring drylands: hard ground, patchy hope
nature-eco-524.text: Restoring a dryland is hard. Rain is rare and variable, heat is high, soils are poor and invasive species spread. Dryland restoration is deliberate work to help degraded drylands recover, either by restoring their former function or by preventing further decline. The IUCN and IPCC stress ecosystem restoration as a tool for slowing climate change and adapting to it. The IUCN also counts restoration as one of the three pillars of {{ref:nature-nbs-220}}. Techniques target the patchy vegetation typical of drylands. Some plant small patches meant to spread ({{ref:nature-eco-525}}) or encourage soil animals. Others plant trees, fence out grazing animals, combine trees with livestock, or build semicircular bunds, low earth banks that catch runoff. The FAO offers 10 practice principles to guide ecosystem restoration.

nature-eco-529.title: Local knowledge in restoring drylands
nature-eco-529.text: Dryland communities have combined trees, crops and livestock successfully for centuries. Restoration builds on that experience when it uses local and indigenous knowledge and community involvement. Case studies find that involving indigenous knowledge and local communities makes restoration more successful. Indigenous fire practices, for example, can lower fuel loads and help prevent large, devastating fires.
